newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN fears outbreak of epidemics, cholera in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: UN fears outbreak of epidemics, cholera in Rwanda.

text.p: The U.N. health agency said on Tuesday it feared epidemics could break out among the weakest among the flood of Hutu refugees returning to Rwanda and warned that cholera remained a big risk.

"The current health situation is grave. These people are hungry, they haven't had food and good water for a long time and they are exhausted," Ebrahim Samba, head of Africa division at the World Health Organisation (WHO) told a Geneva briefing.
"This is ideal ground for an explosion of diseases -- malaria, diarrhoea, infections."

In one of the biggest homeward refugee movements in recent history, half a million Rwandan Hutus poured out of east Zaire's Goma region after Tutsi rebels shelled a camp and forced Hutu militiamen to flee. Many aid agencies were caught off-guard.
WHO said two cases of cholera had been reported on Sunday at the hospital in Rwanda's northwestern border town of Gisenyi, the main entry point. There were also confirmed cases in Goma.

A cholera outbreak claimed more than 30,000 lives in Goma in 1994 when Rwandan Hutu refugees fled after a Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis. At the peak of the epidemic, more than 5,000 people died in a single day.
David Heymann, a WHO specialist, said his agency feared a cholera outbreak among the returning refugees.

"Cholera is there. It has been confirmed and the potential for it to spread through Rwanda is very big," he said. "For every one case visible, there could be a hundred other cases that are not visible."
WHO said its medical stocks in the region were enough to cope immediately with 5,000 cases of cholera.

Primary sources of cholera infection are contaminated drinking water and food prepared by infected persons. Preventive actions include cholorination of wells, boiling water for cooking and building pit latrines.
Treatment involves rehydration to replace water and salts lost through severe diarrhoea and vomiting. Severe cases require intravenous rehydration and treatment with antibiotics.
Samba said WHO also feared malaria could be potentially a bigger killer than cholera. A WHO medical team was on its way tor Gisenyi on Tuesday for a full assessment of the returnees' health needs.
Samba joined the U.N. refugee agency and several aid organisations in urging the deployment of a multinational force to back up the aid effort.

He said WHO had no assessment of the health situation in Bukavu further south, where Tutsi rebels are denying access to aid agencies trying to reach another half million refugees scattered in forests, hills and banana plantations.

"The health situation is very unpredictable and changing," he said. "I'll be in support of a force. They are organised, they have equipment, transport, food and medicine. They are able-bodied fit young people. They can be extra pairs of hands."
